issues.legal_issue: A written dispute-resolution clause is a valid arbitration agreement when its substance demonstrates a mandatory intention to arbitrate, even if it does not expressly state that the arbitral decision is final and binding.
material_facts: The parties signed a development agreement containing a written clause requiring disputes arising from or relating to the agreement to be referred to arbitration.
The clause provided for appointment of a sole arbitrator by mutual agreement, with an alternative process involving party-appointed arbitrators and a third arbitrator.
The clause selected the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as the law governing the arbitration.
One party invoked the clause and applied to the court for appointment of an arbitrator after the other party did not respond.
The clause did not expressly use the words “final and binding,” but did not specifically exclude the binding nature of arbitration.
issues.conclusion: The clause was a valid arbitration agreement, and the application for appointment of an arbitrator was maintainable. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s decision was set aside, and a sole arbitrator was appointed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(1)(b) and 7 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 require an agreement in writing to submit disputes arising from a defined legal relationship to arbitration, but prescribe no particular form of words. The substance of the clause and the parties’ intention govern: a mandatory reference to arbitration can establish an obligation to arbitrate and to abide by the tribunal’s decision even without the express words “final and binding,” absent a specific exclusion of an essential attribute. Rukmanibai Gupta v. Collector, Jabalpur recognizes that an arbitration agreement need not take a particular form; K.K. Modi v. K.N. Modi identifies the attributes of arbitration, including an intended binding decision; Encon Builders and Jagdish Chander distinguish a mandatory obligation to arbitrate from a mere possibility or future option; and Enercon (India) Ltd. v. Enercon GmbH supports a pragmatic, common-sense approach that gives effect to the parties’ intention. Section 11 provides for court appointment of an arbitrator where the requirements for appointment are met.

rule.if: arbitration_appointment_proceeding and written_clause_mandates_arbitration and clause_provides_arbitrator_selection_process and clause_selects_arbitration_governing_law and not clause_excludes_binding_arbitration

predicates.arbitration_appointment_proceeding: A party asks a court to appoint an arbitrator under a purported arbitration clause.
predicates.written_clause_mandates_arbitration: The parties have a written clause requiring covered disputes to be referred to arbitration.
predicates.clause_provides_arbitrator_selection_pro: The clause sets out a process for selecting the arbitrator or arbitrators.
predicates.clause_selects_arbitration_governing_law: The clause selects a law to govern the arbitration.
predicates.clause_excludes_binding_arbitration: The clause expressly excludes the binding nature of the arbitral decision or another essential attribute of arbitration.

issues.definition: When a party seeks court appointment under a written clause that requires arbitration, provides a selection process, selects arbitration law, and does not exclude binding arbitration, the clause is treated as valid and the appointment application as maintainable.
